UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                  BEFORE THE
                    FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

                                                    )
    Northern Indiana Public Service Company         )
    LLC v. Midcontinent Independent System          )          Docket No. EL26-36-001
    Operator, Inc.                                  )
                                                    )


    REQUEST FOR REHEARING OF THE SIERRA CLUB, ENVIRONMENTAL LAW &
      POLICY CENTER, CITIZENS ACTION COALITION OF INDIANA, CITIZENS
             UTILITY BOARD OF WISCONSIN, AND PUBLIC CITIZEN


         Pursuant to Section 313(a) of the Federal Power Act (“FPA”) and Rule 713 of the Rules

of Practice and Procedure of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (“Commission” or

“FERC”),1 Sierra Club, the Environmental Law & Policy Center, Citizens Action Coalition Of

Indiana, Citizens Utility Board Of Wisconsin, and Public Citizen (collectively “Public Interest

Organizations” or “PIOs”) respectfully submit this request for rehearing of the Commission’s

March 19, 2026 Order (“Order”) in the above-captioned proceeding, granting Northern Indiana

Public Service Company LLC’s (“NIPSCO”) complaint against the Midcontinent Independent

System Operator (“MISO”).2

I.       Introduction

         NIPSCO brought its complaint in response to the Department of Energy (“DOE” or “the

Department”) order issued December 23, 2025 directing Schahfer Units 17 and 18 to operate

past their planned retirement dates (“December DOE Order”).3 The DOE Order was issued

  N. Ind. Pub. Serv. Co. v. Midcontinent Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc., 194 FERC ¶ 61,215 (2026).

  Department of Energy Order No. 202-25-12 (Dec. 23, 2025). The DOE has since issued a second order

                                                   1
 pursuant to Section 202(c) of the Federal Power Act (“FPA”), but did not comply with the

requirements the FPA mandates for such orders, and improperly disregarded the resource

adequacy efforts and findings of state authorities, MISO, and this Commission, which together

had already ensured that MISO North and Central regions have sufficient capacity.4 Numerous

parties, including many of the PIOs, have challenged the December DOE Order in the United

States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit.5 As PIOs explained in their initial

protest (“PIOs’ Protest”), the Commission’s Order exacerbates the Department’s mistakes and

further violates the FPA by approving cost recovery for the Schahfer plant in a manner that does

not ensure costs will be allocated commensurate with benefits.6 PIOs request that the

Commission grant rehearing to 1) respond to PIOs’ arguments that Schahfer Unit 18 provides no

benefits, and is not used and useful; 2) explain what benefits the Schahfer units provide that

remain uncompensated under the current tariff; 3) revisit the Commission’s treatment of the

Schahfer units as capacity resources despite clear language in the DOE Orders prohibiting such

consideration; and 4) explain how demand-based load ratio share properly matches costs to

benefits.

II.      Request for Rehearing

          A.     Statement of Issues

      1. The Order is arbitrary and capricious, unsupported by substantial evidence, and not the
         product of reasoned decision-making because it failed to respond to substantial questions
         raised by PIOs in the proceeding. 5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A); Bloomberg L.P. v. SEC, 45 F.4th
         462, 476−77 (D.C. Cir. 2022) (“[A]n agency’s response to public comments must be


4

Environmental Council, Environmental Law and Policy Center, and Public Citizen, Motion to Intervene
and Request for Rehearing and Stay of DOE Order No. 202-25-12 (Jan 22, 2026), available at
https://www.energy.gov/ceser/federal-power-act-section-202c-schahfer-order-no-202-25-12.
5
  Petition for Review, Sierra Club v. DOE, Case No. 26-1056 (D.C. Cir. 2026).
6
  PIOs Protest, Docket No. EL26-36-000, Accession No. 20260120-5232 (Jan. 20, 2026). Public Citizen
did not join the PIOs Protest, but joins this request for rehearing.


                                                 2
        sufficient to enable the courts to see what major issues of policy were ventilated and why
       the agency reacted to them as it did.”) (cleaned up).
    2. The Order exceeds the Commission’s jurisdiction and statutory authority by violating
       FPA Section 202(c)’s requirement that rates be just and reasonable, which encompasses
       the principle that utilities that pay for a facility must benefit from that facility’s operation.
       16 U.S.C §§ 824a, 824d(a); Illinois Com. Comm’n v. FERC, 576 F.3d 470, 476 (7th Cir.
       2009) (“FERC is not authorized to approve a pricing scheme that requires a group of
       utilities to pay for facilities from which its members derive no benefits, or benefits that
       are trivial in relation to the costs sought to be shifted to its members.”); K N Energy, Inc.
       v. FERC, 968 F.2d 1295, 1300 (D.C. Cir. 1992) (“[I]t has been traditionally required that
       all approved rates reflect to some degree the costs actually caused by the customer who
       must pay them.”).
    3. The Order is arbitrary and capricious, unsupported by substantial evidence, and not the
       product of reasoned decision making for reaching a conclusion regarding the
       beneficiaries of the Schahfer units’ continued operation that has no rational basis in the
       record. 5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A); 16 U.S.C. § 825l(b). See also, Motor Vehicle Mfrs. Ass’n of
       U.S., Inc. v. State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co., 463 U.S. 29, 43 (1983); PPL Wallingford
       Energy LLC v. FERC, 419 F.3d 1194, 1198 (D.C. Cir. 2005); FPL Energy Maine Hydro
       LLC v. FERC, 287 F.3d 1151 (D.C. Cir. 2002); California Pub. Utils. Comm’n v. FERC,
       20 F.4th 795, 802 (D.C. Cir. 2021); Delaware Div. of Pub. Advoc. v. FERC, 3 F.4th 461,
       469 (D.C. Cir. 2021).
    4. The Order is arbitrary and capricious, unsupported by substantial evidence, and contrary
       to law under Section 202, 16 U.S.C § 824d(a), for seemingly relying on the Department’s
       unlawful emergency declaration as the sole basis for the conclusion that an emergency
       exists in the MISO North and Central zones and that there is a shortage of capacity in
       these zones, in spite of clear evidence to the contrary. 5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A).

        B.      Argument in Support of Rehearing

                1.      The Commission failed to engage with PIOs’ evidence that Schahfer Unit
                        18 is not providing benefits.

        As PIOs previously explained, Schahfer Unit 18 has not been operational since before the

issuance of the December DOE Order.7 PIOs Protest argued that no costs associated with

Schahfer Unit 18 should be allocated to any MISO customer for two reasons: First, any costs

incurred to repair Unit 18 are imprudent because the DOE does not have authority under section

202(c) to require NIPSCO to revive a non-operational generation facility.8 As PIOs argued,


7
  PIOs Protest at 17. PIOs understand that Schahfer Unit 18 continues to be non-functional. See IURC
March 2026 Public Meeting, comments of Vince Parisi, President and COO of NIPSCO available at
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uXEwNQdi3r0 (advance video to 3:45:19).
8
  PIOs Protest at 17−18.


                                                   3
 expenses undertaken based on an illegal interpretation of a 202(c) order are facially imprudent.

Second, PIOs argued that NIPSCO should not be able to seek cost recovery for Unit 18 while it

is not functional and unable to provide any benefits to the MISO region.9 While the Commission

responded to the first argument, it failed to respond to the second.10

       The Commission has long held that, in general, utilities may only charge ratepayers for

expenses that are “used and useful.”11 While the Commission is able to and has departed from

the used and useful standard, it must make a showing that doing so “reasonably balances

consumers’ interest in fair rates against investors’ interest in maintaining financial integrity and

access to capital markets.”12

       The used-and-useful standard is a distinct standard from prudence. In fact, courts have

explained that exceptions to the used-and-useful standard are sometimes justified because

expenditures that are not used and useful can be prudent.13 Thus the Order’s statement that

“arguments related to the prudence of costs associated with operating the Schahfer Units … are

beyond the limited scope of this proceeding” does not address PIOs’ arguments.14 The tariff

provisions that the Commission blessed would allow NIPSCO to seek recovery for expenditures

at Schahfer Unit 18 before the plant becomes used and useful. The Commission may impose an

exception to the used-and-useful standard to allow recovery of prudent costs for the non-used

plant, but it must justify this decision. At a minimum, the Commission would need to answer the

how projects costs and Allowance for Funds Used During Construction are added to rate base only when
a project is used and useful).
12
   La. Pub. Serv. Comm’n v. FERC, 174 F.3d 218, 229 (D.C. Cir. 1999) (citing Town of Norwood v.
FERC, 80 F.3d 526, 531 (D.C. Cir. 1996)) (cleaned up).
13
   See id. (discussing how prudent but canceled investments are not presently used and useful).
14
   Order at P 40.


                                                  4
 threshold question whether doing so reasonably balances consumers’ interest in fair rates against

investors’ interest, before—presumably in a later proceeding—deciding which expenses incurred

for the unused unit were prudent. By only speaking to the question of prudency and not why the

Commission is departing from the used and useful standard, the Commission failed to respond to

an important component of PIOs’ Protest and did not meet its burden for reasoned decision

making under the Administrative Procedure Act (“APA”).15


                2.      The Commission does not justify its reading of the DOE Orders to allow
                        consideration of Schahfer as a capacity resource.

        The DOE Orders are clear: Schahfer Units 17 and 18 “shall not be considered capacity

resources.”16 As PIOs explained, the most straightforward reading that respects this requirement

would prohibit the Commission from treating the units as capacity resources.17 And without the

ability to recognize a capacity benefit from the units, it is not just and reasonable for the

Commission to assign costs associated with Schahfer units’ capacity value to any MISO

participants. The Commission’s response to PIOs’ citation of the December DOE Order was to

ascribe an entirely different directive to the December DOE Order: that the Schahfer units cannot

be counted as capacity resources in the MISO resource adequacy construct, but are to be

considered capacity resources in every other respect.18 But the Commission’s sole justification

for its reading, which goes against the plain language of the December DOE Order, is that the

December DOE Order cited resource adequacy concerns as the justification for the order. DOE’s

   See Bloomberg L.P. v. SEC, 45 F.4th 462, 476−77 (D.C. Cir. 2022) (“[A]n agency’s response to public
comments must be sufficient to enable the courts to see what major issues of policy were ventilated and
why the agency reacted to them as it did.”) (cleaned up).
16
   December DOE Order at 5; March DOE Order at 9.
17
   PIOs Protest at 9−10.
18
   Order at P 41.



                                                   5
 stated overarching basis for its order, however, is no reason to ignore the plain language of its

directive: the units “shall not be considered capacity resources.”19 The Commission must either

provide a valid justification for its strained interpretation of the actual language of the DOE

Orders, or it must state why it does not believe the DOE Orders’ discussion of capacity roles for

the Schahfer Units is binding.20

                3. The Commission has not explained why over-procurement of capacity
                   provides a benefit to ratepayers or what benefits remain uncompensated
                   under the current tariff.

        Even putting aside the clear language of the DOE Orders, PIOs provided evidence that

the Schahfer units did not provide a capacity benefit to MISO customers because each zone in

MISO had already met its capacity obligation.21 The Commission did not address this argument

in its Order, instead stating that DOE “indicat[es] that resource adequacy concerns for [zones

1−7] were the driver for the DOE Order.”22 But the Commission has also previously recognized

that over-procuring capacity can lead to unjust and unreasonable rates,23 and that the amount of

capacity MISO requires customers to source under its resource adequacy construct is just and

reasonable.24 The Commission’s Order here undermines those previous findings by forcing

customers to pay for capacity greater than that required by the MISO resource adequacy

construct, without offering any reasoning for its departure from previous Commission orders.

20
   FCC v. Prometheus Radio Project, 592 U.S. 414, 423 (2021) (“The APA’s arbitrary-and-capricious
standard requires that agency action be reasonable and reasonably explained.”).

   PIOs Protest at 9−10 and n.33.
22
   Order at P 37.
23

Commission rejected tariff revisions because “it would require ratepayers to pay twice for the same
capacity need and would result in over-procuring capacity”).
24
   Midcontinent Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc., 189 FERC ¶ 61,065 (2024) (accepting the MISO resource
adequacy construct).



                                                     6
 The Commission must explain itself to the extent it departs from its previous reasoning in order

to meet its obligations under the APA.25


        The Commission also failed to adequately respond to PIOs’ argument that current tariff

provisions fully compensate Schahfer for any cognizable benefits it may provide MISO

customers.26 The Order states that “[w]hile existing Tariff provisions govern the distribution of

market revenues for any energy supplied by Market Participants, they do not provide a cost

allocation method for prudently incurred costs associated [sic] orders issued under FPA section

202(c).”27 But that statement is nonresponsive to the argument in PIOs Protest, which focuses on

compensation for actual benefits provided. Neither the Commission in its Order nor NIPSCO in

its protest have explained what benefits the Schahfer units provide that are not already

compensated through existing tariff mechanisms. It is unjust and unreasonable for customers to

be allocated costs that are not associated with commensurate benefits.28 The fact that the current

tariff does not permit recovery of 202(c) order compliance costs is irrelevant if the tariff already

provides adequate compensation for all of the benefits Schahfer provides.




25
   FCC v. Fox TV Stations, Inc., 556 U.S. 502, 515 (2009) (agencies must provide reasoned explanation for
departing from prior policies).
26
   PIOs Protest at 8−12.
27
   Order at P 40.
28
   Id. at P 35; Old Dominion Elec. Coop. v. FERC, 898 F.3d 1254, 1263 (D.C. Cir. 2018) (“[I]n order to
ensure just and reasonable rates, FERC must make some reasonable effort to match costs to benefits.”); El
Paso Elec. Co. v. FERC, 76 F.4th 352, 356 (5th Cir. 2023) (“The FPA requires that all rates and charges
made, demanded, or received by any public utility for or in connection with the transmission or sale of
electric energy be just and reasonable. For decades, the FERC and the courts have understood this
requirement to incorporate a cost-causation principle.”) (cleaned up); Long Island Power Auth. & Long
Island Lighting Co. v. FERC, 27 F.4th 705, 709 (D.C. Cir. 2022) (“To be just and reasonable, rates must
‘reflect to some degree the costs actually caused by the customer who must pay for them.’ This ‘cost-
causation principle’ requires ‘comparing the costs assessed against a party to the burdens imposed or
benefits drawn by that party.’” (citing Midwest ISO Transmission Owners v. FERC, 373 F.3d 1361, 1368
(D.C. Cir. 2004)) (cleaned up).



                                                   7
         In fact, the Schahfer Units are not providing capacity benefits as understood in the

context of MISO. Capacity obligations provide an important planning value, for reliability.29 But

if the Schahfer Units are unable to participate in MISO’s capacity construct then it is not clear

what capacity planning value the units can possibly provide. And, as PIOs have previously

discussed, the units’ real-time reliability contribution is already compensated through Value of

Lost Load (“VOLL”) pricing.30 As such, it remains entirely unclear what uncompensated

benefits the Schahfer units are providing.

     4. The Commission has not explained how demand-based load ratio share properly
        allocates costs according to benefits.

        PIOs’ Protest explained that a just cost-allocation mechanism must identify benefits, and

then match benefits to beneficiaries.31 The Commission’s response to PIOs’ arguments fails to

resolve significant questions as to how demand-based load ratio share will accurately allocate

costs according to benefits. PIOs recognize that this proceeding does not determine what, if any,

costs can be recovered. But the tariff language and cost allocation decisions the Commission

makes in this proceeding will provide guideposts for more fact-specific inquiries down the line,

which will help determine the justness and reasonableness of the specific costs and cost

allocation that are determined in those later proceedings. Clear Commission findings identifying

what benefits the units might provide, and who those benefits might accrue to, is critical to

ensure actual costs are ultimately allocated commensurate with benefits.




29

(2022) (“MISO's capacity construct is designed to not only place capacity requirements on LSEs to
promote resource adequacy in a given Planning Year, but also to produce price signals that promote long-
term resource adequacy and economic efficiency.”).
30

31

                                                   8
        As noted in PIOs Protest, the relative benefit each of MISO zones 1−7 will receive from

the delayed retirement of the Schahfer units remains unclear, as does the reasonableness of

allocating costs among zones 1−7 using a demand-based load ratio share methodology.32 The

Order does not provide a reasoned response to this argument. While the Commission stated that

it found a load-ratio-share methodology based on peak demand to be justified in a parallel

proceeding regarding cost allocation for the Campbell plant while it operates pursuant to a 202(c)

order,33 the Campbell order did not explain why load ratio share properly allocated costs

amongst the zones. Instead, the Campbell order provided reasoning why costs should be

allocated on a demand, rather than energy, basis, and summarily stated that “forecasted Season

coincident peak demand for Local Resource Zones 1-7 for the duration of the DOE Order (and

any extensions) … reasonably aligns with the emergency described in the DOE Order and the

beneficiaries of the emergency energy provided by the Campbell Plant.”34 This cursory statement

lacks sufficient reasoning to meet the APA’s requirement that the Commission explains its

reasoning in this docket.35

       It is also not clear why the Commission’s conclusion in the Campbell proceeding should

apply in this proceeding. In the Campbell proceeding, the Commission agreed with intervenor

Consumer Alliance that the costs associated the Campbell plant’s 202(c) order should be

allocated on a demand basis “because the costs relate to capacity.”36 But in the case of the

Campbell plant, the relevant 202(c) order was silent regarding whether the Campbell plant could

                                                  9
 be considered a capacity resource. Here, by contrast, the 202(c) order prohibits considering

Schahfer as a capacity resource, which as explained above dramatically reframes the benefits

Schahfer can realistically provide to the MISO system.

        Moreover, the record in this proceeding contains no evidence that benefits from the

Schahfer units will accrue roughly proportionate to zonal peak demand. Each zone has different

amounts of uncleared capacity and a different level of reliance on capacity imports from other

zones.37 Even if zones 1−7 were short on capacity and the Schahfer units were required to

supplement existing generation capacity on the system, zones with larger quantities of excess

capacity would presumably need less of the capacity from the Schahfer units than zones with less

excess capacity. Thus, even then the benefits would not track with zonal peak demand but rather

would be inversely proportional to uncleared capacity. Furthermore, to the extent that the plants

are needed to meet future demand, allocating costs using current zonal demand is unjustified as

it is the future peak load contributions and available resource levels that will dictate future

capacity needs.38

        Finally, even putting aside the fact that the units are not authorized to provide capacity

services, allocating all costs on a demand basis still may not be justified because it does not

capture all of the units’ benefit streams. PIOs noted that at least Unit 17 may be providing

energy benefits by virtue of its participation in MISO-run energy markets.39 Any revenue from

                                                    10
 the Schahfer units’ participation in the energy and ancillary services markets untethers the

ultimate cost of the units from any resource adequacy benefit they may be providing, making it

even less tenable to allocate costs based on a demand rather than energy basis.

           In making these arguments, PIOs are not trying to pre-judge the prudence of any incurred

costs. Rather, these concerns point to situations in which the rigid cost allocation mechanism that

NIPSCO proposed and the Commission approved will result in an unjust and unreasonable

allocation of costs that might otherwise be prudent. Because the Commission has failed to

identify the benefits the Schahfer units provide, these conflicts are all but inevitable. It is also

why, as discussed in PIOs’ Protest, a hearing is warranted.40

III.       Conclusion

           For the reasons given above, PIOs respectfully request that the Commission grant

rehearing to revisit the proposed recovery for both Schahfer units and to provide updated

guidance on how to calculate the beneficiaries of their delayed retirement.
